clinicalPearls: Renovascular disease is a specifically treatable 'secondary' cause of hypertension because restoring renal perfusion pressure can reverse the pressor pathways it activates (Harrison 22e p.2150).

Roughly 90% of renovascular hypertension is due to atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis (ARAS), which is typically unilateral with a discrete lesion near the renal artery origin in older patients with a broader atherosclerotic risk profile (Harrison 22e p.2139, 2150).

Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) accounts for a minority of cases and characteristically affects younger patients aged ~15 to 50, predominantly women; lesions are more diffuse with an irregular 'sawtooth/string-of-beads' appearance located in the distal renal artery (Harrison 22e p.2139, 2150).

FMD should be suspected with abrupt-onset hypertension (especially in young women) or resistant/recently worsening hypertension; ARAS should be suspected in older patients with other ASCVD evidence or otherwise unexplained decline in kidney function (Harrison 22e p.2139).

Critical stenosis (usually >70 to 80% luminal obstruction) reduces perfusion pressure, activating the renin-angiotensin system, reducing sodium excretion, and engaging sympathetic pathways (Harrison 22e p.2150).

Early renovascular hypertension is angiotensin-dependent and marked by widely varying pressures, loss of circadian BP rhythm, and accelerated target organ injury including left ventricular hypertrophy and renal fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.2150).
An abdominal renal artery bruit, or carotid/femoral bruits, may be audible and supports the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2139, 2150).

When large-vessel disease primarily threatens kidney function the entity is termed ischemic nephropathy; gradually reduced flow can leave function reduced but stable for years, whereas advanced disease produces cortical hypoperfusion and overt tissue hypoxia (Harrison 22e p.2150).

ARAS commonly coexists with preexisting small-vessel disease from hypertension, aging, and diabetes; nearly 85% of patients considered for revascularization already have stage 3 to 5 CKD (eGFR <60) (Harrison 22e p.2150).
The presence of ARAS independently predicts cardiovascular morbidity and mortality regardless of whether revascularization is performed (Harrison 22e p.2150).

Atheroembolic renal disease most often follows arterial procedures (e.g., coronary angiography), with cholesterol crystals lodging in downstream microvessels; manifestations typically appear 1 to 14 days after the inciting event (Harrison 22e p.2152).

Thromboembolic renal disease can cause flank pain, fever, leukocytosis, nausea and vomiting, and a transient extreme rise in LDH if infarction occurs; bilateral involvement causes precipitous functional decline and reduced urine output (Harrison 22e p.2153).
harrison.pathophysiology: The renal cortex receives high arteriolar flow in excess of its metabolic needs for filtration, while the postglomerular medullary circulation has lower flow yet high oxygen consumption, leaving the deeper medulla near the margin of hypoxemia. Large-vessel occlusive disease (atherosclerosis, fibromuscular dysplasia, dissection, extrinsic compression, aortic stent graft) reduces perfusion pressure to the kidney. Once stenosis is hemodynamically significant (typically >70 to 80% lumen occlusion), the drop in perfusion pressure activates the renin-angiotensin system, reduces sodium excretion, and stimulates sympathetic adrenergic pathways, producing angiotensin-dependent systemic hypertension. Sustained pressure and ischemia drive endothelial injury (reflected by increased urinary albumin excretion), microvascular proliferation in early atherosclerosis and later microvascular rarefaction in chronic ischemia, with consequent tubulointerstitial fibrosis and loss of function. In atheroembolic disease, cholesterol crystals from fractured plaque occlude microvessels leaving a characteristic 'cleft' on biopsy (Harrison 22e p.2150-2152).
infectionMimics: Renal infarction from septic emboli (e.g., subacute bacterial endocarditis vegetations)
Thrombotic renal occlusion precipitated by systemic infection such as COVID-19
nonInfectiousMimics: Renal parenchymal disease causing secondary hypertension
Cholesterol atheroembolism mimicking vasculitis (livedo reticularis, eosinophilia, elevated ESR, hypocomplementemia)
additionalInvestigations: Duplex (Doppler) ultrasonography: peak systolic renal artery velocity >200 cm/s suggests >60% occlusion (some trials use >300 cm/s to reduce false positives); renal resistive index informs kidney viability but is operator-dependent
Contrast-enhanced CT angiography: excellent vascular images and assessment of accessory/distal vessels; stents do not cause artifacts; small contrast toxicity risk
Magnetic resonance angiography: non-nephrotoxic but gadolinium is avoided when eGFR <30 due to nephrogenic systemic fibrosis risk; cannot visualize stented vessels
Captopril renography (99mTc-MAG3): strong negative predictive value when entirely normal; limited utility with advanced atherosclerosis or creatinine >2.0 mg/dL
Intraarterial (digital subtraction) angiography: gold standard for large-vessel disease, often performed at time of planned intervention
Plasma renin activity is subject to timing, drugs, and sodium intake and does not reliably predict response to revascularization; renal venous renin sampling is now rarely used due to false results
Kidney biopsy: confirms atheroembolic disease (cholesterol-crystal cleft in microvessels)
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or resistant hypertension failing optimal medical therapy
Progressive decline in GFR during BP treatment, or decline associated with ACE inhibitor/ARB therapy
Recurrent flash pulmonary edema / congestive heart failure not explained by LV dysfunction
Abrupt-onset hypertension in a young woman (suggests FMD) or worsening kidney function in an older patient with ASCVD (suggests ARAS)
New worsening hypertension and deteriorating renal function days after an arterial/angiographic procedure (atheroembolism), possibly reaching a malignant phase
Acute flank pain with fever and markedly elevated LDH suggesting renal infarction; anuria with bilateral acute occlusion
harrison.prognosis: FMD patients are usually younger with otherwise normal vessels and long life expectancy and often respond well to angioplasty; FMD seldom threatens kidney function. Untreated ARAS progresses in nearly 50% of cases over 5 years, sometimes to total occlusion, though intensive BP and statin therapy slow progression. After endovascular stenting renal function recovers in only ~25%, is unchanged in ~50%, and deteriorates in the remainder. ARAS independently predicts cardiovascular events and death. Atheroembolic renal disease carries an ominous prognosis with 1-year mortality exceeding 38%; untreated malignant hypertension historically had 1-year mortality over 90% (and >50% at 6 to 12 months with target organ injury), but current 5-year survival exceeds 50% with effective antihypertensive therapy (Harrison 22e p.2150-2154).
pitfalls: Plasma renin activity is transient and influenced by drugs/sodium/timing, so it does not reliably predict response to revascularization; over-reliance on it is misleading (Harrison 22e p.2151).

Multiple randomized trials show no compelling benefit of revascularization over optimal medical therapy for moderate ARAS regarding BP or renal function over 3 to 5 years; revascularization should not be assumed beneficial just because flow is restored (Harrison 22e p.2139, 2150).
Revascularization rarely normalizes BP alone because most patients have preexisting hypertension and need continued drug therapy (Harrison 22e p.2150).
Atheroembolic complications of revascularization can be catastrophic and accelerate the very hypertension and renal failure the procedure intended to prevent (Harrison 22e p.2151).

Atheroembolic renal disease is frequently underdiagnosed and is often a diagnosis of exclusion; systemic features (fever, abdominal pain, weight loss) are present in fewer than half of patients (Harrison 22e p.2152).

Hypertensive nephrosclerosis is often assigned without specific etiologic proof; nephrosclerosis changes also occur with aging, dyslipidemia, and glucose intolerance with only modest association with BP, and antihypertensive therapy does not alter its course (Harrison 22e p.2154).
harrison.severityClassification: No formal staging is given; severity is gauged by degree of luminal stenosis (hemodynamically critical at >70 to 80% occlusion), CKD stage (most revascularization candidates are stage 3 to 5 with eGFR <60), and clinical syndrome (stable medically managed disease versus rapidly progressive/resistant disease). Table 289-2 outlines clinical factors favoring revascularization plus medical therapy (progressive GFR decline, medical failure of BP control, GFR decline with ACEi/ARB, recurrent unexplained heart failure) versus medical therapy with surveillance (controlled BP with stable function, stable non-progressing stenosis, advanced age/limited life expectancy, high atheroembolic risk, concomitant parenchymal disease with proteinuria) (Harrison 22e p.2152).
management: Control blood pressure with renin-angiotensin system blockade using an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker, monitoring renal function and potassium closely, especially in bilateral disease
Slow atherosclerotic progression with a statin, antiplatelet therapy and smoking cessation in atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis
Offer percutaneous transluminal angioplasty for fibromuscular dysplasia, which is often curative in younger patients
Reserve angioplasty with stenting for atherosclerotic stenosis in selected cases such as resistant hypertension, flash pulmonary oedema or progressive renal impairment
Add further antihypertensive agents as needed and manage overall cardiovascular risk
Monitor blood pressure, renal function and stent patency, and involve vascular and interventional specialists for revascularisation decisions
